title-group.article-title: Meta-analysis of probiotic effects on broiler performance: Bacillus outperforms Lactobacillus with enhanced and longer efficacy in developing regions

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Probiotics are increasingly investigated as sustainable alternatives to antibiotic growth promoters in poultry production, with Bacillus and Lactobacillus being the most extensively studied genera. However, performance responses remain inconsistent across studies, probiotic genera, and production settings. This meta-analysis quantified the overall effects of probiotics on broiler growth performance, with particular emphasis on genus-specific responses and study-level moderators of feed conversion ratio (FCR). Following PRISMA guidelines, 53 studies comprising 106 independent trials were included. Random-effects models were used to estimate mean differences, and heterogeneity was assessed using Q, τ², and I² statistics. Meta-regression and subgroup analyses evaluated potential moderators, including probiotic genus, dose, trial duration, breed, feed type, probiotic configuration, and regional economic status. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and adjusted using the Duval and Tweedie trim-and-fill method. Overall, probiotic supplementation significantly improved body weight (66.61 g, P < 0.001), feed intake (29.80 g, P = 0.002), and FCR (0.058, P < 0.001). After adjustment estimates increased for body weight (78.34 g), feed intake (61.42 g), and FCR (0.107). Probiotic genus, trial duration, and regional economic classification were identified as significant moderators of FCR (P < 0.05). Subgroup analyses indicated that Bacillus-based probiotics were associated with more consistent improvements in FCR across production stages (days 21, 35, and 42), whereas Lactobacillus-based effects showed a transient effect limited to day 21. Probiotic-associated improvements in FCR were more pronounced in studies conducted in developing regions. Overall, the findings support that probiotics enhance broiler performance, with Bacillus providing superior and sustained efficacy, supporting its strategic use as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Broiler production faces increasing pressure to maintain high growth performance while reducing reliance on antibiotic growth promoters and addressing concerns related to antimicrobial resistance. In this context, probiotics have gained attention as complementary or alternative nutritional strategies to improve gut health, nutrient utilization, and productivity in poultry systems (Sachdeva et al., 2025; Idowu et al., 2025). Probiotics can modulate intestinal microbiota, enhance gut barrier function, and improve digestive efficiency, which may ultimately support growth performance and feed efficiency in broiler chickens (Idowu et al., 2025; Naeem and Bourassa, 2025). However, despite widespread research and commercial use, probiotic responses in broilers remain inconsistent across studies, indicating that their efficacy depends not only on probiotic characteristics but also on environmental conditions, management practices, and production systems (Wang et al., 2024; Hashemitabar and Hosseinian, 2024). This variability becomes particularly relevant when comparing studies conducted under different regional and production circumstances.

Several experimental studies have reported positive effects of probiotic supplementation on feed conversion ratio (FCR), BW, and feed intake (FI) (Idowu et al., 2025), however, others have observed neutral (Olnood et al., 2015) or even negative effects (Bajagai et al., 2016). For instance, Bacillus and Lactobacillus are among commonly used genera in poultry nutrition (Bajagai et al., 2016), differing in survivability, colonization potential, and mode of action. Individual studies have reported varying effects for both genera on growth performance and feed conversion ratio (Wang et al., 2024; Attia et al., 2023; Mazanko et al., 2022). Such variation may arise from differences in probiotic strain identity, dosage, timing of administration, host factors, feed composition, and environmental conditions (Naeem and Bourassa, 2025). In addition, production environments may differ substantially between regions in terms of microbial challenge, climatic stress and hygiene practices, all of which may influence the magnitude of probiotic responses in broiler chickens. Consequently, individual studies may provide limited insight into broader patterns of probiotic efficacy across production systems.

Meta-analysis is a powerful and widely used statistical technique for synthesizing data from multiple independent studies to provide a comprehensive and quantitative summary of the available evidence (El-Fateh et al., 2024). By combining results from different studies, meta-analysis increases statistical power, improves estimates of the effect size, and helps identify patterns or sources of variability among study outcomes (Borenstein et al., 2021). Moreover, meta-analysis can explore the influence of moderators through meta-regression and subgroup analyses, contributing to a deeper understanding of factors affecting treatment efficacy or performance outcomes. In poultry research, meta-analytical approaches have been increasingly applied to evaluate nutritional interventions and to identify factors that influence growth performance and feed efficiency.

Although probiotics are widely promoted as alternatives or complements to antibiotic growth promoters, the relative effectiveness of different probiotic genera and the contextual factors that influence their performance effects in broiler chickens remain insufficiently quantified. It was hypothesized that probiotic efficacy differs among probiotic genera and is influenced by study characteristics such as trial duration, probiotic formulation, dose, and production context. Therefore, the objective of this study was to quantify the effects of probiotic supplementation on broiler BW, FI, and FCR using a meta-analytical approach, and to determine whether probiotic genus, probiotic configuration, dose, trial duration, breed, feed type, and regional context explain variation in FCR responses.

sec.title: Criteria for study selection
sec.p: This meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the overall effects of probiotic supplementation on broiler performance parameters, including BW, FI, and FCR. To be included, all studies were required: (i) to be from broilers over 1-day-old, (ii) to have received a probiotic during the entire treatment period, and (iii) to have available information on the BW, FI, and FCR while they were receiving probiotics. The initial studies were reviewed, and the references were searched for other possible studies. After identification, studies were screened and selected depending on the available information. The complete list of studies and related data can be found in Tables (Supplementary Table S1 and S2).

sec.title: Outcomes and definitions
sec.p: Supplementation with probiotics was analysed as a tool which may improve BW, FI and FCR in broilers. When the study included more than one probiotic group or different doses of the same probiotic, each probiotic group was compared with the control group separately. Further, the probiotic effect in the starter period, which was 7, 14 or 21 days, clumped together under 21 days. The ‘mixed’ probiotic subgroup in subgroup analyses included combinations of multiple genera (e.g., Bacillus, Lactobacillus, Enterococcus, Pediococcus, Saccharomyces) and therefore should be interpreted as a general representation of multi-genus probiotic formulations rather than a specific Bacillus–Lactobacillus blend. The standard deviation from different reports was used in this study for meta-analysis. For any studies that failed to provide SD, the SEM was used to calculate SD by multiplying the standard error of mean with the square root of the sample size.

Mortality was not included as an outcome because it was not reported consistently across the included studies in a form suitable for pooled quantitative synthesis. The predefined primary outcomes of the present analysis were growth-related performance variables. FCR values were extracted as reported in the original studies. Information on whether feed conversion ratio was corrected for mortality was not reported consistently and is therefore acknowledged as a limitation. Information on probiotic recovery levels, route of administration, anticoccidial use, and background antimicrobial exposure was also not reported consistently enough across studies to be analyzed systematically.

sec.title: Literature search, study selection and data extraction
sec.p: Relevant studies published from January 2021 to December 2024 were identified through comprehensive searches of the NCBI PubMed (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed), Web of Science (http://www.webofknowledge.com), and Google Scholar (http://scholar.google.com). The literature search was restricted to studies published between January 2021 and December 2024 to reflect contemporary broiler production systems, probiotic formulations, and post-antibiotic growth promoter regulatory conditions, thereby enhancing the relevance and comparability of the included evidence. A systematic literature search was conducted using combinations of the following keywords: “broiler” OR “poultry” OR “chicken”, “probiotic”, “Bacillus” OR “Lactobacillus”, and “growth performance” OR “body weight” OR “feed intake” OR “feed conversion ratio” OR “feed efficiency”. Studies were included if they evaluated probiotic supplementation in broiler chickens and reported at least one production performance outcome (body weight, feed intake, or feed conversion ratio). Only original in vivo trials with a control group were considered eligible for quantitative synthesis. Studies involving layers, breeders, disease-challenge models, were excluded. The study selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram.

where wirepresents the weight assigned to each study, τ2represents the between-study variance, i represents the index for each individual study, and n represents the sample size. All analyses were conducted using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software version 4 following the methodology described by Borenstein et al. (2021). To ensure consistent interpretation of effect direction across outcomes, the sign of the MD was defined such that positive values always favored probiotic supplementation, whereas negative values favored the control. Accordingly, in the forest plots, effect sizes located on the right side (positive MD) indicate superiority of probiotics, while those on the left side (negative MD) indicate superiority of the control. To maintain this directional consistency, MD for BW and FI were calculated as Probiotic over Control, because higher values represent improved performance. In contrast, for FCR, where lower values indicate better efficiency, MD were calculated as Control over Probiotic. This approach ensures that improvements in FCR attributable to probiotics are represented as positive effect sizes.

The results (Forest plots) are presented as MD between the probiotic treatment and controls with 95% CI using a random effects model. The studies in the analysis are assumed to be a random sample from a universe of potential studies, and this analysis will be used to make an inference to that universe. Publication bias was evaluated using Egger’s regression test and visual inspection of funnel plots. Where significant bias was observed, Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill method was applied to adjust the effect size estimates.

sec.title: Assessment of heterogeneity
sec.p: In this study, FCR that encompass both body weight and feed intake was used further in downstream analyses. Heterogeneity in the effect sizes of FCR was detected using Cochran’s Q test. The Q-statistic was used to test the null hypothesis that all studies in the analysis share a common effect size. The criterion alpha of 0.10 was used to reject the null hypothesis that the true effect size is the same in all studies. Other metrics such as Tau-squared (τ²) and predictive intervals were used to quantify heterogeneity (DerSimonian and Laird, 2015) and determine the anticipated dispersion of true effects in future studies (Higgins et al., 2009), respectively. In addition, the I-squared statistic was applied, which provides information that the variance in observed effects reflects variance in true effects rather than sampling error (Borenstein, 2020).

sec.title: Meta-regression and subgroup analyses
sec.p: To investigate potential sources of heterogeneity in FCR, a meta-regression analysis was conducted. The model assessed the relationship between several covariates including breed type, feed type, trial duration, probiotic genus, probiotic configuration, and the economic status of the study country. For categorical variables, dummy coding was applied, with Cobb (breed type), corn–soy (feed type), day 35 (trial duration), Lactobacillus (probiotic genus), single strain (configuration), and developed regions (economic status) serving as reference categories. Furthermore, a priori subgroup analyses were planned to examine factors that could potentially influence the magnitude of the FCR related with Lactobacillus and Bacillus: (1) General effect of genera used (Lactobacillus versus Bacillus versus mixed), (2) Effect of dosage, (3) Effect of study duration (day 21 versus day 35 verses day 42), and (4) effect of country economic status/region (developed verses developing regions).

Countries or regions were classified as developed or developing according to United Nations economic classification (United Nations., 2024) applied at the country or region level. This variable was used as a study-level moderator in meta-regression and subgroup analyses. Because this classification was applied at the study level rather than within controlled head-to-head experimental comparisons, regional findings were interpreted as contextual associations rather than direct causal comparisons.

sec.title: Overview of included studies
sec.p: The literature search across PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar yielded a large number of papers on probiotics in poultry (a total of 1,131 records were identified across databases). After screening, 53 studies, encompassing 106 independent trials, were included in the meta-analysis. These studies were published between January 2021 and December 2024 and focused on randomized controlled trials in healthy broilers with probiotic supplementation throughout the treatment period. All studies reported at least one of the primary outcomes: BW, FI, and FCR.

sec.title: Excluded studies
sec.p: Of the initial papers identified in the literature search, a substantial number were excluded after screening titles, abstracts, and full texts. Exclusions were primarily due to failing to meet inclusion criteria: studies not involving broilers (e.g., layer chickens or other poultry), those not providing probiotics throughout the entire treatment period, or not reporting data on BW, FI, or FCR. Additional reasons included non-randomized or non-controlled designs, studies on diseased or stressed birds (e.g., challenge trials with pathogens), duplicate publications, non-peer-reviewed sources (e.g., conference abstracts or gray literature), and irrelevant outcomes (e.g., focusing only on gut health without performance metrics). The detailed breakdown of excluded studies, including numbers at each PRISMA stage (identification, screening, eligibility), is provided in the PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1).

sec.title: Effect of probiotics on BW, FI and FCR of broiler chickens
sec.p: From the 53 included studies, a total of 81, 66, and 100 experiments provided usable data for body weight, feed intake, and feed conversion ratio, respectively. Across the included studies, probiotic supplementation was associated with improved growth performance. In the pooled estimate, probiotics increased BW compared to controls (MD = 66.61 g, 95% CI 51.92 to 81.31; Predictive Interval (PI)= 66.61, 95% CI −51.77 to 184.99; P < 0.001) in the random effects model (Figure 2). Regarding FI, probiotics increased FI compared to controls (MD = 29.80 g, 95% CI 10.74 to 48.86; PI = 29.80, 95% CI −116.66 to 176.25; P = 0.002) in the random effects model (Figure 3). Similarly, regarding FCR, broilers fed with probiotics had improved FCR in comparison with those without probiotic supplementation (MD = 0.058, 95% CI 0.037 to 0.078; PI = 0.058, 95% CI −0.110 to 0.226; P < 0.001) in the random effects model (Figure 4).

sec.title: Heterogeneity and meta-regression analyses
sec.p: Heterogeneity occurred among experiments (Q-statistic: the Q-value was 2079.80 with 99 degrees of freedom and P < 0.001; I2-statistic: 95.67%). The genera, duration of experiment and economic status were associated with FCR (P = 0.013, P < 0.001, and P = 0.026, respectively) while breed, feed type, and probiotic configuration (P = 0.483, P = 0.067, and P = 0.326, respectively) were not significantly associated with FCR in the meta-regression analysis (Table 1). Among probiotic genera, Bacillus (coefficient = 0.099, P = 0.001) and Lacticaseibacillus (coefficient = 0.176, P = 0.024) supplementation were linked to improved FCR, while other genera showed no statistically significant effects. Longer trial duration (42 days) was negatively associated with FCR (coefficient = –0.119, P < 0.001), whereas studies conducted in developing economies (coefficient = 0.097, P = 0.026) showed significant positive association. The overall model fit was statistically significant (Q = 48.83, df = 15, P < 0.001). However, residual heterogeneity remained high (τ² = 0.0068, I² = 92.2%, Q = 1078.3, df = 84, P < 0.001) while comparing with the null model (τ² = 0.0070, I² = 95.2%), suggesting that, though certain moderators were significant, substantial between-study variability remained unexplained.

caption.p: Summary of Meta-regression analysis for independent variables that influenced the feed conversion ratio of broilers between probiotic supplementation and control (Difference in means). Values for individual covariates and as sets (Genus and Breed) are mentioned.

sec.title: Subgroup Analyses
sec.p: Subgroup analyses indicated that Bacillus-based probiotics were associated with improved FCR (MD = 0.104; 95% CI 0.074 to 0.134; τ² = 0.005; P < 0.001), but Lactobacillus based supplementations did not show a significant effect on FCR (MD = −0.017, 95% CI −0.101 to 0.066; τ² = 0.030; P = 0.684). The mix of probiotic genera showed relatively reduced but significant improvement in FCR (MD = 0.070, 95% CI 0.008 to 0.133; τ² = 0.012; P = 0.027) (Figure 5). The effect of dosage of both Bacillus and Lactobacillus on FCR could not reach statistically significant level, however their direction of effect was opposite. The Bacillus group showed a negative coefficient (−0.0178, P = 0.083) reflecting that higher dosage will have negative effect on FCR (Figure 6) while Lactobacillus showed a positive coefficient (0.0732, P = 0.121) on FCR (Figure 7) describing higher dosage will benefit FCR. In duration-based subgroup analyses, Bacillus-associated improvements in feed conversion ratio were detected across the evaluated production stages, whereas Lactobacillus-associated improvement was observed only at the earlier stage and was not sustained at later time points. In this regard, the Bacillus effect at days 21, 35 and 42 was (MD = 0.056, 95% CI 0.016 to 0.097; τ² = 0.003; P = 0.006), (MD = 0.155, 95% CI 0.096 to 0.215; PI −0.089 to 0.400; τ² = 0.012; P < .001), and (MD = 0.024, 95% CI 0.008 to 0.041; PI −0.022 to 0.071; τ² = 0.001; P = 0.003), respectively. Similarly, Lactobacillus showed effect on days 21 (MD = 0.021, 95% CI 0.001 to 0.041; PI −0.011 to 0.031; τ² = 0.001; P = 0.039), 35 (MD = −0.023, 95% CI −0.056 to 0.010; PI −0.000 to 0.000; τ² = 0.000; P = 0.172) and 42 (MD = 0.002, 95% CI −0.131 to 0.135; PI −0.478 to 0.482; τ² = 0.039; P = 0.977). In the same manner the multi-genus probiotic formulations showed effect on days 21 (MD = 0.093, 95% CI 0.060 to 0.126; PI 0.023 to 0.164; τ² = 0.001; P < 0.001), 35 (MD = 0.102, 95% CI 0.019 to 0.186; PI −0.172 to 0.377; τ² = 0.014; P = 0.017) and 42 (MD = 0.020, 95% CI −0.082 to 0.123; PI −0.329 to 0.369; τ² = 0.013; P = 0.700) (Figure 8, A, B and C).

sec.p: In subgroup analyses based on regional economic classification, probiotic-associated improvements in feed conversion ratio were more pronounced in studies conducted in developing regions than in studies conducted in developed regions. Within both regional groupings, Bacillus-based probiotics showed a more favorable numerical pattern than Lactobacillus-based interventions; however, the number of studies from developed regions was limited, and these results should be interpreted cautiously as study-level contextual associations rather than direct comparisons. In this regard, developing regions showed better response (MD = 0.061, 95% CI 0.039 to 0.082; P < 0.001) than developed regions (MD = 0.022, 95% CI 0.002 to 0.043; P = 0.031). Furthermore, in developing regions (Figure 9A) the response of Bacillus probiotics (MD = 0.111, 95% CI 0.079 to 0.143; P < 0.001) was statistically significant than Lactobacillus probiotics (MD = −0.022, 95% CI −0.118 to 0.073; P = 0.646). A similar response observed in developed regions (Figure 9B), though the number of studies here were not sufficient, where Bacillus probiotics effect on FCR of broilers was significant (MD = 0.023, 95% CI 0.001 to 0.046; P = 0.043) than Lactobacillus (MD = 0.018, 95% CI −0.028 to 0.065; P = 0.435).

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: A significant publication bias was observed for BW (Figure 10A), FI (Figure 10B) and FCR (Figure 10C), as confirmed by Egger’s test (P < .05). Applying the Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill methods identified missing studies and provided adjusted point estimates for BW, FI and FCR as 78.34 with 95% confidence interval (64.22 to 92.46), 61.42 with 95% confidence interval (43.93 to 78.90), and 0.107 with 95% confidence interval (0.081 to 0.133), respectively.

caption.p: (A-C). Funnel plots illustrating publication bias assessment for body weight (A), feed intake (B), and feed conversion ratio (C). The X-axis represents the mean differences (effect size) between probiotic and control groups, while the Y-axis shows the corresponding standard error for each study. Symmetry of the plot indicates low publication bias, whereas asymmetry suggests potential bias among included studies. The circles represent observed (blue) and imputed studies (red) while blue and red signs on X-axis reflects the original and corrected (through Dual and Tweedie trim-and-fill method) effect sizes, respectively.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The present meta-analysis indicates that probiotic supplementation is generally associated with improved broiler growth performance, supporting the view that probiotics can function as useful nutritional tools in modern poultry production. At the same time, the results show that probiotic efficacy is not uniform and depends on both biological and contextual factors. This variability helps explain why individual studies often report inconsistent performance responses despite evaluating interventions under the same broad label of “probiotics.” These findings reinforce the growing consensus that probiotics can effectively enhance growth performance. For example, a recent systematic review highlights how probiotics modulate gut microbiota balance, suppress pathogens, and strengthen gut barrier function, contributing to better nutrient absorption and growth (Idowu et al., 2025). The consistent positive effects observed in our aggregated data also align with more recent in vivo investigations: for instance, Zhang et al. (2025) reported that a composite probiotic formulation significantly enhanced growth performance and intestinal health in broilers. Ren et al. (2025) further demonstrated that both in ovo and continuous probiotic supplementation improved performance outcomes in broilers. These converging lines of evidence support the notion that probiotics, when properly selected and administered, can act as viable alternatives to antibiotic growth promoters.

A clear genus-related pattern emerged in the synthesis. Bacillus-based probiotics showed more consistent associations with improved FCR than Lactobacillus-based interventions. A plausible explanation is that many Bacillus strains are spore formers, which may improve stability during feed processing and storage and enhance survival through the upper gastrointestinal tract (Kimelman and Shemesh, 2019). By contrast, Lactobacillus-based responses may depend more strongly on strain identity, viability, delivery conditions, and the production environment, which could contribute to the less consistent results observed across studies. These observations align with existing literature reporting high variability and, sometimes, an absence of positive growth performance results for Lactobacillus supplementation in poultry (Tsega et al., 2024). For instance, lack of a significant effect of Lactobacillus acidophilus on growth performance has been observed (Attia et al., 2023), while another study using encapsulated Lactobacillus paracasei also reported no significant improvement in growth performance (Gyawali et al., 2022). Conversely, the strong positive effect observed for Bacillus strains is supported by multiple studies showing that Bacillus supplements, such as Bacillus subtilis and Bacillus licheniformis, significantly promote desirable metrics like body weight, average daily weight gain, and FCR (Wang et al., 2023). In addition, the finding that the mix of multi-genera probiotics was effective but yielded a lesser effect than Bacillus alone is particularly noteworthy, suggesting a potential lack of synergy or even competitive inhibition among the strains rather than additive or synergistic benefits. Probiotic blends based on multiple strains are often developed with the goal of achieving superior outcomes compared to single strains; however, the complex compatibility and interactions among strains are known variables (Al-surrayai et al., 2022). This observed pattern, where the combined effect is attenuated relative to the best-performing single component (Bacillus), is directly supported by research studying combinations of these two genera. For instance, in one experiment investigating the effects of B. subtilis and Lactobacillus additives in heat-stressed broilers, researchers concluded that there was no synergistic effect when the two were used together, and the effectiveness of the strains used separately was significantly greater than that of the combination (Wang et al., 2024). However, opposite results have also been reported. One study evaluating probiotics under heat stress conditions found that while Bacillus enhanced growth, Lactobacillus alone, or in combination with Bacillus, yielded stronger effects on final body weight and body weight gain compared to Bacillus alone (Hashemitabar and Hosseinian., 2024). Such contrasting findings underscore the complexity of probiotic efficacy, often attributing to differences in strain type, dosage, age of birds, or environmental stressors.

The time-related subgroup findings also suggest that probiotic responses are dynamic across the production cycle. The more sustained association observed for Bacillus may reflect greater persistence or functional stability over time, whereas the more limited early-stage response associated with Lactobacillus may indicate benefits that are more dependent on early colonization, starter-phase conditions, or short-term microbial interactions. This suggests that Bacillus-based probiotics provide a more consistent and sustained benefit to feed efficiency throughout the broiler production cycle (Cirilo et al., 2023). The enduring efficacy of Bacillus strains, often encompassing species like B. subtilis and B. licheniformis, is widely supported in the literature, where they are frequently reported to significantly improve FCR. For example, studies found that B. subtilis supplementation resulted in a significantly lower FCR compared to controls across the entire study period, 35 days (Yu et al., 2024) or 42 days (Murshed et al., 2024). This prolonged efficacy may be linked to their robust spore-forming and encapsulation capabilities, allowing them to survive the harsh gastrointestinal environment and colonize the intestine (Mazanko et al., 2022). This study also observed that effect of Bacillus probiotics on FCR reaches to its peak by day 35 and then start to decline later. Qin et al. (2024) reported a similar effect where they found a significant effect of B. licheniformis on FCR between days 1-35 followed by no significant effect on FCR between days 35-70. This reflects that no probiotics groups (control) attain the same growth levels with time, around 42 days, as of Bacillus probiotics and minimize differences between control and probiotic groups in terms of FCR. A similar pattern of host response to probiotics and fecal microbiota transfer was observed previously in terms of microbiome (Bilal et al., 2021b), bone and immunity related parameters (Bilal et al., 2025). In contrast, the transient and early-stage efficacy observed for Lactobacillus (significant only at Day 21) is consistent with studies showing that while some Lactobacillus strains may improve FCR during the starter phase (Day 1-21), these benefits often diminish or become non-significant during later and overall periods (Wu et al., 2019). In another study, involving encapsulated Lactobacillus paracasei found FCR decreased significantly in the starter phase (1-21 days), but no notable improvement was observed in the finisher phase (22-42 days) (Gyawali et al., 2022). The efficacy of Lactobacillus in improving growth performance and FCR can be inconsistent, with many studies reporting no significant effect, possibly due to factors like the specific strain used, viability issues, dose rate, or hygienic measures. Therefore, these findings support the view that probiotic effects should not be generalized across the entire broiler cycle without considering genus and duration of supplementation.

The more pronounced probiotic-associated responses observed in studies conducted in developing regions may reflect differences in baseline production conditions, including hygiene pressure, heat stress, diet variability, and pathogen challenge. Under such circumstances, there may be greater potential for probiotics to improve gut function and performance. However, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because the regional variable was applied as a study-level contextual moderator rather than as a direct experimental comparison between production systems. Accordingly, the results indicate context dependence rather than definitive superiority of probiotic supplementation in one region over another. The pattern, where probiotics show positive effects under suboptimal rearing (Bilal et al., 2021a) or when the diet is deficient in essential nutrients (Golshahi et al., 2025), is consistent with observations in the literature. Developing regions often present greater environmental and hygienic stressors, which challenge broiler health. The improved FCR observed in response to probiotics in developing regions supports the notion that they successfully mitigate the negative impacts of prevalent stressors, which may include enteric disorders like necrotic enteritis (Acharya et al., 2024) or Eimeria infection (Memon et al., 2022). Further, dissecting the results by genus reveals that Bacillus strains exhibited a potent FCR-improving effect, which was significant in developing regions in comparison with Lactobacillus. This differential effect underscores that growth-promoting additives generally show more pronounced positive effects under suboptimal rearing conditions, suggesting the Bacillus contribution is most evident when environmental pressures are high and basal performance is depressed. This durability is due to the strains' robust spore-forming and protective extracellular matrix forming capabilities (Kimelman and Shemesh, 2019) and their ability to continuously secrete digestive enzymes, enhancing feed efficiency. Nonetheless, the numerically superior performance of Bacillus compared to Lactobacillus in developed regions suggests an advantage even under good sanitary conditions, aligning with frequent documentation of Bacillus significantly improving FCR (Mazanko et al., 2022). While studies related with Lactobacillus often report inconsistent or non-significant effects on growth performance (Attia et al., 2023). The reliably stronger response of Bacillus supports its strategic use as an alternative to antibiotics in regions facing major environmental stresses.

In this meta-analysis, a significant level of heterogeneity was detected across studies, indicating that the impact of probiotics on feed conversion ratio (FCR) in broilers is not uniform but influenced by study-level moderators. Meta-regression analysis identified probiotic genus, trial duration, and the economic status of the study location as significant predictors of FCR outcomes. These findings suggest that both biological determinants (e.g., taxonomic and functional variation between probiotic strains) and production-related conditions (e.g., trial duration and resource availability in different production systems) contribute to the observed variability. Despite these significant associations, the model explained a small portion of observed heterogeneity, with a high residual τ² and I² indicating that much of the variability remains unexplained. The modest R² analog underscores that while certain genera and trial conditions are associated with improved FCR, the broader variability in the literature limits predictive certainty. These highlights the complexity of probiotic–host–environment interactions. Similar patterns have been reported in another meta-analysis, which emphasize that strain-level differences, duration of the experiments, number of broilers, year of publication and administration route of probiotics had an impact on the production parameters while explaining a small percent of heterogeneity (Blajman et al., 2014). Further, the predictive interval in our analysis indicated an overall positive effect of probiotics on FCR in future studies, however, the wide interval also encompassed negligible or even negative effects of probiotics. This uncertainty in outcomes also point out to probiotic efficacy that is context-dependent and shaped by different factors including strain specificity, dosage, administration methods, environmental conditions, storage stability, and interactions with other feed additives (Naeem and Bourassa, 2025). These insights underscore the need to move beyond broad taxonomic categorizations toward more precise, strain-specific evaluations accompanied by standardized experimental designs.

Further, a significant publication bias was detected across all three production parameters (body weight, feed intake, and feed conversion ratio), suggesting that smaller or non-significant studies may be underrepresented in the published literature. To address this issue, the Duval and Tweedie “trim-and-fill” method was applied, which imputes potentially missing studies and recalculates adjusted pooled effects. After adjustment, the positive impacts of probiotics on all three parameters were further strengthened, indicating that the observed benefits are robust and not solely attributable to selective reporting. Funnel plot asymmetry and other methods are useful tools for detecting small-study effects, which are often interpreted as potential evidence of publication bias. However, publication bias is only one of several possible explanations for asymmetry. Further, the trim and fill methods in presence of between-study heterogeneity may be biased. Therefore, the estimates from these methods should be considered with caution.

An additional limitation concerns the representativeness of the included studies for commercial poultry production. Many experimental trials are conducted under relatively controlled conditions that may not fully capture the pathogen challenge, stocking density, management variability, and feed-manufacturing conditions encountered in commercial operations. As a result, extrapolation of probiotic effects from small-scale trials to commercial practice should be made with caution. Further, other methodological limitations should be considered when interpreting the results of this meta-analysis. First, the calculation of feed conversion ratio (FCR) was not standardized across studies. Most studies used the conventional feed intake-to-body weight gain ratio. A few studies incorporated mortality-adjusted values, while others did not clearly report how mortality was handled. Second, reporting of antimicrobial additives and anticoccidial compounds in basal diets was inconsistent. Many studies explicitly excluded these additives, while a few still included commercial anticoccidials. Others provided only general descriptions such as “antibiotic-free.” Third, verification of probiotic recovery or viability in the final feed or water was reported only in a limited number of studies, and most reported only the intended probiotic dosage. Finally, although in-feed supplementation was the predominant delivery method, a few studies used alternative routes such as waterline administration, or oral gavage. Because these variables were inconsistently reported across studies, they could not be incorporated as moderator variables in the meta-analysis. Nevertheless, the large dataset and the use of random-effects models allowed robust estimation of overall probiotic effects while accounting for substantial between-study heterogeneity.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta-analysis show that probiotic supplementation was associated with improved body weight, feed intake, and feed conversion ratio in broilers. The magnitude of response varied across studies and was influenced by probiotic genus, trial duration, and regional economic classification. Among the evaluated probiotic groups, Bacillus-based products showed the most consistent association with improved feed conversion ratio across production stages, whereas Lactobacillus-based effects were less consistent over time. Probiotic-associated improvements in feed conversion ratio were more pronounced in studies conducted in developing regions, although this finding should be interpreted as a study-level contextual association rather than a direct regional comparison. Overall, the results support probiotics as useful nutritional tools in broiler production while highlighting the need for more standardized reporting of probiotic recovery, route of delivery, mortality-adjusted feed conversion ratio, background antimicrobial or anticoccidial use, and commercial-scale study descriptors. Future work should explore additional factors to explain variability and refine strain-level and dose-specific recommendations to optimize consistent performance responses.
